## Overview

Sudden oak death, caused by the water mould *Phytophthora ramorum*, has killed
millions of tanoaks and oaks in coastal California and Oregon since the
mid-1990s. Its spores are splashed and blown from infected foliage, mostly a
few metres, occasionally kilometres, and only in wet, mild weather.
@Meentemeyer2011 modelled its spread across California from 1990 to 2030 on a
grid of 250 m cells, each holding up to 100 units of host vegetation,
susceptible or infected. Infected units release spores when the weather and
the season allow; the spores travel by a mixture of a short-range and a
long-range dispersal kernel, and infect susceptible units where they land.
They predicted a ten-fold increase in infection between 2010 and 2030, much
more in favourable weather, and little benefit from curbing long-distance
spread once the disease is established.

This implementation is an **adaptation**. The source's statewide maps of host
vegetation and weekly weather were never published, so it runs on a
synthetic landscape with synthetic weather, and reproduces the source's
qualitative results rather than its areas.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## Dispersal

A spore travels in a random direction a distance drawn from a Cauchy kernel,
with scale 20.57 m with probability `γ = 0.9947` and 9.5 km otherwise. On
cells of 250 m, a spore released at a cell's centre lands in each cell with
probability given by `sod_kernel`:

```{julia}
short = sod_kernel(20.57; radius=4)
long = sod_kernel(9504; radius=99)
(short_in_own_cell=round(short[5, 5]; digits=3),
 short_within_1km=round(sum(short); digits=3),
 long_within_12km=round(sum(long[(100 - 49):(100 + 49), (100 - 49):(100 + 49)]);
                        digits=2))
```

As the source says, nearly all spores stay close: about nine in ten
short-range spores land in their own cell (93% in the source). The rare
long-range spores spread over tens of kilometres.

Because each infected unit releases a Poisson number of spores and each lands
independently, the spores landing in a cell are Poisson, with a mean that is
the sum over all infected cells of their spores times the probability of
landing there: a convolution. The model computes it as two kernel fields of
the core package, the long-range one by fast Fourier transform, on a torus
twice the landscape's size whose padding is masked, so spores leaving the
landscape are lost.

## Landscape and weather

The synthetic landscape is 100 × 100 cells (25 × 25 km). Half the cells hold
host vegetation, in clusters; a third of the forest is redwood-tanoak, the
rest mixed evergreen. Redwood-tanoak forest takes part in transmission from
January to September, mixed evergreen from February to September.

```{julia}
prob = problem(:sudden_oak_death; seed=1)
n = 100
hosts = prob.u0.S[1:n, 1:n] .+ prob.u0.I[1:n, 1:n]
p1 = heatmap(Float64.(hosts); c=:Greens, aspect_ratio=1, title="host units",
             titlefontsize=10, xticks=false, yticks=false)
p2 = heatmap(Float64.(prob.u0.forest[1:n, 1:n]);
             c=cgrad([:white, :darkgreen, :olive], 3; categorical=true), aspect_ratio=1,
             title="redwood-tanoak (dark), mixed (light)", titlefontsize=10,
             xticks=false, yticks=false, colorbar=false)
w = prob.p.weather
p3 = plot(1:52, reshape(w[1:(52 * 4)], 52, 4); lw=1.5, xlabel="week",
          ylabel="weather index", label=permutedims(string.(1990:1993)),
          title="weekly weather, 1990-1993", titlefontsize=10, legendfontsize=7)
plot(p1, p2, p3; layout=(1, 3), size=(950, 300), left_margin=3Plots.mm,
     bottom_margin=4Plots.mm)
```

Each week's weather index is the share of its days with rain times the
source's suitability of its mean temperature for sporulation; it enters both
at the source of the spores and where they land. The source used kriged
weather at 250 m for 1990 to 2008. Here a coastal climate is drawn at
random: wet, mild winters and springs, dry summers, and wetter and drier
years. Its overall wetness is the one choice made to match the source: with
it, infection grows about ten-fold from 2010 to 2030.

## An epidemic, 1990 to 2030

The pathogen arrives at three cells near the centre in 1990, each with one
infected unit. Six runs:

```{julia}
function epidemic(; snapshots=(), kwargs...)
    integ = init(problem(:sudden_oak_death; kwargs...); save_everystep=false)
    area = Float64[]
    maps = Dict{Int,Matrix{Float64}}()
    for year in 1990:2030
        for _ in 1:52
            step!(integ)
        end
        push!(area, sod_infected_area(integ.u))
        year in snapshots && (maps[year] = Float64.(integ.u.I[1:n, 1:n]))
    end
    return area, maps
end
ensemble(; seeds=1:6, kwargs...) =
    fetch.([Threads.@spawn first(epidemic(; seed=s, kwargs...)) for s in seeds])
_, maps = epidemic(; seed=1, snapshots=(2000, 2010, 2020, 2030))
plot([heatmap(maps[y]; c=:inferno, clims=(0, 100), aspect_ratio=1, title="$y",
              titlefontsize=10, xticks=false, yticks=false)
      for y in (2000, 2010, 2020, 2030)]...; layout=(1, 4), size=(1000, 230))
```

```{julia}
random = ensemble()
A = reduce(hcat, random)
p = plot(1990:2030, A; color=:gray, alpha=0.6, label="", xlabel="year",
         ylabel="infected area (km²)", yscale=:log10, ylims=(0.05, 400))
plot!(p, 1990:2030, mean(A; dims=2); color=:black, lw=2, label="mean", size=(650, 340))
```

```{julia}
(area_2010=round(mean(A[21, :]); digits=1), area_2030=round(mean(A[41, :]); digits=1),
 increase=round(mean(A[41, :]) / mean(A[21, :]); digits=1))
```

Infected units multiply locally, cell by cell, while the rare long-range
spores start new foci kilometres away, which then grow in turn. The
infected area grows about ten-fold from 2010 to 2030, as in the source,
though here over a landscape of 300 km² of forest rather than California's.

## Weather scenarios

The source ranks its observed years by their total weather index and draws
the years after 2008 at random from the better half (favourable), the worse
half (unfavourable), or all of them (random). Six runs each:

```{julia}
scenarios = Dict(w => reduce(hcat, ensemble(; weather=w))
                 for w in (:favourable, :random, :unfavourable))
p = plot(; xlabel="year", ylabel="infected area (km²)", size=(650, 340), legend=:topleft)
for (w, c) in ((:favourable, 2), (:random, :black), (:unfavourable, 1))
    plot!(p, 1990:2030, mean(scenarios[w]; dims=2); lw=2, color=c, label=string(w))
end
p
```

```{julia}
(favourable=round(mean(scenarios[:favourable][41, :]); digits=1),
 random=round(mean(scenarios[:random][41, :]); digits=1),
 unfavourable=round(mean(scenarios[:unfavourable][41, :]); digits=1))
```

As in the source, the weather after 2008 makes a large difference by 2030:
favourable weather gives several times the infection of unfavourable (about
five-fold in the source), and random weather a little over half that of
favourable (half in the source).

## Curbing long-distance spread

The source asks what reducing long-distance dispersal from 2009 would achieve,
for example by stopping the movement of infected plants. Multiplying the
long-range share of spores by 0.5, 0.1 or 0.01:

```{julia}
curbs = Dict(f => reduce(hcat, ensemble(; management=(2009, f))) for f in (0.5, 0.1, 0.01))
p = plot(1990:2030, mean(scenarios[:random]; dims=2); lw=2, color=:black,
         label="unchanged", xlabel="year", ylabel="infected area (km²)", size=(650, 340),
         legend=:topleft)
for (k, f) in enumerate((0.5, 0.1, 0.01))
    plot!(p, 1990:2030, mean(curbs[f]; dims=2); lw=2, color=k, label="long range × $f")
end
p
```

```{julia}
(unchanged=round(mean(scenarios[:random][41, :]); digits=1),
 curbed=[round(mean(curbs[f][41, :]); digits=1) for f in (0.5, 0.1, 0.01)])
```

Curbing long-distance spread slows the epidemic but does not stop it: the
foci already established keep growing and merging by short-range spread, and
even a hundred-fold cut leaves about half the infected area by 2030. The source
finds a smaller benefit, about a third less.
